questions.q: What is a database transaction?
options: A logical unit of work consisting of one or more database operations
A physical disk sector
A database username
A type of index
questions.explanation: A transaction groups operations into a logical unit that should satisfy database correctness properties.

questions.q: Which ACID property means a transaction is all-or-nothing?
options: Consistency
Isolation
Atomicity
Durability
questions.explanation: Atomicity ensures that either all operations of a transaction take effect or none do.

questions.q: Which ACID property ensures that a committed transaction survives a system crash?
options: Isolation
Durability
Atomicity
Consistency
questions.explanation: Durability requires committed changes to persist despite failures, typically using logging and stable storage.

questions.q: Which ACID property ensures that a transaction takes the database from one valid state to another?
options: Isolation
Durability
Atomicity
Consistency
questions.explanation: Consistency means integrity constraints remain satisfied when a transaction commits.

questions.q: Which ACID property controls the visibility of concurrent transaction operations?
options: Isolation
Durability
Consistency
Atomicity
questions.explanation: Isolation prevents concurrent execution from producing effects that violate the chosen isolation guarantees.

questions.q: What is a schedule in transaction processing?
options: A list of database users
An ordering of operations from one or more transactions
A backup calendar only
A list of index pages
questions.explanation: A schedule specifies the order in which transaction read, write, commit and abort operations execute.

questions.q: When is a schedule serial?
options: When every operation is a write
When transactions execute in alternating steps
When each transaction completes before the next one begins
When all transactions abort
questions.explanation: A serial schedule runs transactions one after another without interleaving their operations.

questions.q: What is a non-serial schedule?
options: A schedule with no transactions
A schedule containing only commits
A schedule with one operation
A schedule in which operations of different transactions are interleaved
questions.explanation: A non-serial schedule interleaves operations from multiple transactions.

questions.q: What does conflict serializability test?
options: Whether a schedule can be transformed into a serial schedule by swapping non-conflicting operations
Whether every transaction uses a primary key
Whether all transactions read the same row
Whether the database has an index
questions.explanation: Conflict equivalence is based on preserving the order of conflicting operations.

questions.q: When do two operations conflict?
options: They belong to the same transaction
They access different data items
They access the same item, belong to different transactions, and at least one is a write
They are both commit operations
questions.explanation: Conflicts arise for read-write, write-read and write-write pairs on the same data item across transactions.

questions.q: Which pair of operations does not conflict?
options: Read(X) and Write(X)
Read(X) and Read(X)
Write(X) and Read(X)
Write(X) and Write(X)
questions.explanation: Two reads of the same item do not change the value or impose an ordering requirement.

questions.q: What does a precedence graph represent?
options: Database storage locations
User roles and permissions
B-tree parent-child links
Transactions as vertices and conflict ordering as directed edges
questions.explanation: An edge Ti to Tj indicates a conflicting operation of Ti occurs before one of Tj.

questions.q: What indicates that a schedule is conflict-serializable?
options: Its precedence graph is acyclic
Its precedence graph has a self-loop
Every transaction writes one item
It contains no read operations
questions.explanation: A schedule is conflict-serializable exactly when its precedence graph has no directed cycle.

questions.q: If a precedence graph contains a directed cycle, what can be concluded?
options: The schedule is serial
The schedule is conflict-serializable
The schedule is not conflict-serializable
All transactions are read-only
questions.explanation: A directed cycle prevents a topological ordering of transactions and therefore rules out conflict serializability.

questions.q: What is view serializability?
options: A condition based only on transaction names
A weaker serializability notion based on read-from relationships and final writes
A rule requiring all reads before writes
A method for sorting index entries
questions.explanation: View equivalence preserves initial reads, reads-from relationships and the transaction responsible for the final write.

questions.q: Which statement about conflict and view serializability is correct?
options: Every view-serializable schedule is conflict-serializable
The two concepts are identical
No serial schedule is view-serializable
Every conflict-serializable schedule is view-serializable
questions.explanation: Conflict serializability is stricter; every conflict-serializable schedule is view-serializable, but not vice versa.

questions.q: What is a recoverable schedule?
options: A schedule in which a transaction commits only after the transactions whose values it has read have committed
A schedule with no read operations
A schedule in which all transactions commit simultaneously
A schedule that never writes data
questions.explanation: Recoverability prevents a transaction from committing based on data written by an uncommitted transaction.

questions.q: What is a cascading rollback?
options: A transaction is committed twice
A database index is rebuilt
Aborting one transaction forces other dependent transactions to roll back
A transaction reads only committed data
questions.explanation: If a transaction reads uncommitted data from another transaction, the first transaction's abort may require dependent rollbacks.

questions.q: What is a cascadeless schedule?
options: A schedule where all transactions use timestamps
A schedule in which transactions read only values written by committed transactions
A schedule with no writes
A schedule that contains a cycle
questions.explanation: Cascadeless schedules prevent reads of uncommitted writes and therefore avoid cascading aborts.

questions.q: What is a strict schedule?
options: A schedule that permits dirty reads
A schedule where reads always occur before writes
A schedule with no commits
A schedule that prevents other transactions from reading or writing an item written by an uncommitted transaction
questions.explanation: Strictness delays both reads and writes of an item until the transaction holding its write has committed or aborted.

questions.q: What is the basic idea of two-phase locking (2PL)?
options: A transaction has a growing phase for acquiring locks and a shrinking phase for releasing them
A transaction must use exactly two tables
Every transaction commits twice
Locks are acquired only after commit
questions.explanation: In 2PL, locks are acquired during the growing phase and released during the shrinking phase.

questions.q: What is the growing phase of 2PL?
options: The phase in which all locks are released
The phase in which a transaction may acquire locks but may not release any
The phase after a transaction commits
The phase in which only shared locks are allowed
questions.explanation: During the growing phase, a transaction may obtain locks but cannot release locks.

questions.q: What is the shrinking phase of 2PL?
options: The phase in which a transaction acquires new locks
The phase in which the database is backed up
The phase in which a transaction releases locks and cannot acquire new ones
The phase in which SQL is parsed
questions.explanation: Once a transaction releases its first lock, it enters the shrinking phase and cannot obtain additional locks.

questions.q: What is strict 2PL?
options: A protocol that releases all locks before the first write
A protocol that uses no exclusive locks
A protocol that prevents all concurrent reads
A protocol that holds exclusive locks until commit or abort
questions.explanation: Strict 2PL retains exclusive locks until transaction completion, simplifying recovery and preventing cascading rollback.

questions.q: What does a shared lock permit?
options: Reading an item while allowing other compatible shared locks
Writing an item while excluding every other lock
Deleting the database
Changing the transaction timestamp
questions.explanation: Multiple transactions can hold compatible shared locks on the same item to read it.

questions.q: What does an exclusive lock permit?
options: Only other shared locks
Reading and writing while excluding incompatible locks
Only index scans
Only commit operations
questions.explanation: An exclusive lock gives a transaction write access and prevents conflicting access by other transactions.

questions.q: What is a lock upgrade?
options: Changing an exclusive lock to no lock
Changing a timestamp into a lock
Changing a shared lock to an exclusive lock
Releasing every lock at commit
questions.explanation: A transaction may request an upgrade from shared to exclusive when it needs to modify an item.

questions.q: What is deadlock?
options: A transaction finishes before it starts
A database contains duplicate keys
A buffer page is clean
Two or more transactions wait indefinitely for resources held by one another
questions.explanation: Deadlock occurs when transactions form a circular wait and none can proceed.

questions.q: Which graph is commonly used for deadlock detection?
options: Wait-for graph
B-tree graph
Entity-relationship diagram
Query parse tree
questions.explanation: A wait-for graph has transactions as nodes and edges showing which transaction is waiting for another.

questions.q: What does a cycle in a wait-for graph indicate?
options: The database is fully backed up
A possible deadlock among transactions
All locks are compatible
The schedule is serial
questions.explanation: A cycle in the wait-for graph indicates circular waiting and hence deadlock.

questions.q: What is a timestamp-ordering protocol?
options: A protocol that sorts table names alphabetically
A protocol that uses only shared locks
A protocol that orders conflicting operations according to transaction timestamps
A protocol that prevents transactions from reading
questions.explanation: Timestamp ordering assigns each transaction a timestamp and enforces a consistent order on conflicting operations.

questions.q: In timestamp ordering, what does TS(T) represent?
options: The number of tables accessed by T
The number of locks held by T
The disk address of T
The timestamp assigned to transaction T
questions.explanation: TS(T) is the transaction's timestamp, usually assigned when it begins.

questions.q: What does read_TS(X) record?
options: The largest timestamp of any transaction that successfully read X
The smallest value stored in X
The number of reads of X
The timestamp of the database backup
questions.explanation: read_TS(X) tracks the most recent timestamp among successful reads of data item X.

questions.q: What does write_TS(X) record?
options: The number of writes to X
The largest timestamp of any transaction that successfully wrote X
The first value ever stored in X
The lock owner of X
questions.explanation: write_TS(X) records the timestamp of the most recent successful write on X.

questions.q: What is multiversion concurrency control (MVCC)?
options: A method that stores only one version of every row
A method that disables concurrent transactions
A method that maintains multiple versions of data to support concurrent access
A method that replaces SQL with file operations
questions.explanation: MVCC keeps versions so readers can access a consistent snapshot while writers create newer versions.

questions.q: What is a common benefit of MVCC?
options: It eliminates the need for storage
It prevents every possible application error
It guarantees that no transaction can abort
Readers can often proceed without blocking writers
questions.explanation: Readers can use an appropriate committed version while writers update a newer version.

questions.q: What is optimistic concurrency control based on?
options: Assuming conflicts are uncommon and checking for conflicts before commit
Locking every row permanently
Using only hash indexes
Preventing all read operations
questions.explanation: Optimistic control allows work to proceed and validates whether the transaction can safely commit.

questions.q: Which phases are commonly associated with optimistic concurrency control?
options: Parse, compile, execute
Read, validation, write
Lock, unlock, delete
Backup, restore, checkpoint
questions.explanation: A typical optimistic protocol has a read phase, a validation phase and a write phase.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a transaction log?
options: To store only query results
To list database users
To record changes and transaction events needed for recovery
To replace the data files
questions.explanation: The log provides information required to redo or undo operations after failures.

questions.q: What is write-ahead logging (WAL)?
options: Data pages must be written before any log record
The log is discarded after every query
Only read operations are logged
The relevant log record must reach stable storage before the changed data page is written
questions.explanation: WAL ensures recovery information is durable before a modified data page is allowed to reach disk.

questions.q: What is a checkpoint in database recovery?
options: A recovery marker that helps limit how much of the log must be processed after a failure
A command that deletes all old rows
A lock used only for reading
A method for creating a candidate key
questions.explanation: A checkpoint records a recovery position and can reduce restart work.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the REDO operation during recovery?
options: To reverse an uncommitted transaction
To reapply logged updates that should be present after recovery
To remove all indexes
To discard committed transactions
questions.explanation: REDO reapplies updates so committed changes are reflected in the recovered database.

questions.q: What is the purpose of UNDO during recovery?
options: To repeat every committed operation
To create a new transaction timestamp
To reverse effects of transactions that did not commit
To sort the transaction log
questions.explanation: UNDO removes effects of incomplete transactions so the database returns to a consistent state.

questions.q: What is a deferred database modification scheme?
options: Updates are written to the database before they are logged
Every update is immediately visible to all transactions
The log is never used
Database updates are postponed until the transaction commits
questions.explanation: Deferred modification records changes in the log and applies them to the database after commit, often requiring REDO but not UNDO.

questions.q: What is an immediate database modification scheme?
options: Database pages may be updated before commit, so recovery may need both UNDO and REDO
Updates are applied only after a full backup
No log records are written
Only read-only transactions are allowed
questions.explanation: Immediate modification may write uncommitted changes to disk, so recovery must undo incomplete work and redo committed work.

questions.q: What is a database shadow page or shadow copy approach intended to provide?
options: A method for sorting a relation
A recovery approach that preserves an unchanged page mapping while updates are made to new pages
A protocol for granting user roles
A type of SQL injection
questions.explanation: Shadow paging keeps an old consistent page table while modified pages are written separately, then switches the pointer at commit.

questions.q: What is a phantom read?
options: A transaction reads the same row twice and gets the same value
A transaction loses its database password
Repeating a predicate query returns a different set of rows because another transaction inserted or deleted matching rows
A transaction reads an index root
questions.explanation: A phantom occurs when a repeated range or predicate query sees newly matching or missing rows due to concurrent changes.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a serializable isolation level?
options: To permit all dirty reads
To force every query to use a hash index
To disable transactions
To make concurrent execution equivalent to some serial execution
questions.explanation: Serializable isolation aims to ensure the outcome is equivalent to a serial ordering of transactions.

questions.q: What is a lost update problem?
options: One transaction overwrites another transaction's update because of an unsafe interleaving
A transaction reads a committed value twice
A database restores a checkpoint
Two transactions use different tables
questions.explanation: A lost update occurs when concurrent writes cause one transaction's change to be overwritten without being properly accounted for.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a savepoint inside a transaction?
options: To commit the entire database
To mark a point to which part of a transaction can be rolled back
To create a new database user
To rebuild a B+ tree
questions.explanation: A savepoint lets an application roll back part of the current transaction without necessarily aborting all of it.
